summary: Decide whether an integer is a power of two.
mainInsight: A power of two has exactly one set bit, so n & (n - 1) (which clears the lowest set bit) must be 0 - as long as n is positive.

approaches.name: Divide by 2 loop
approaches.summary: Keep halving while divisible; end at 1.

approaches.name: n & (n - 1) == 0
approaches.summary: Positive n with a single set bit.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Single-set-bit test: n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0. Clue: A power of two has exactly one set bit in binary, so clearing the lowest set bit must leave zero.
keyPoints: A power of two has exactly one set bit in binary, so clearing the lowest set bit must leave zero.
cards.explanation: Clearing the only set bit gives zero, while any other positive number keeps a set bit.

rubric.clue: A power of two has exactly one set bit in binary, so clearing the lowest set bit must leave zero.

promptVariants: Which expression tests a power of two in O(1)?
What identity characterises powers of two in binary?
cards.explanation: Exactly one set bit: removing it leaves 0.

incorrectOptionExplanations.n > 0 and n % 2 == 0 (is even): Every even number passes, including 6, which is not a power of two.
incorrectOptionExplanations.n > 0 and n | (n - 1) == 0: n | (n - 1) is at least n, so it is never 0 for n >= 1; the test is always false.
incorrectOptionExplanations.n > 0 and n & (n + 1) == 0: That is true for 1, 3, 7, 15 (all ones) but false for 2 and 4, so it is not a power-of-two test.

promptVariants: Why does n & (n - 1) == 0 imply a power of two?
What happens to the bits of n when you compute n - 1, and why does that reveal a power of two?
cards.answer: n - 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and all the lower zeros to 1. AND with n therefore clears that bit; the result is 0 only when it was the only set bit, i.e. n = 2^k.

promptVariants: Which input falsely passes n & (n - 1) == 0 without the guard?
options: n = 1, which is 2^0 and would wrongly fail
n = 2, since 2 & 1 == 0 makes it fail the test
n = 2^31, which overflows a 32-bit signed integer
cards.explanation: Zero has no set bit and is not a power of two; negatives are also excluded by the guard.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the bit trick: ___
Checking a power of two with n & (n - 1) is ___ time.
cards.explanation: A fixed number of word operations.

promptVariants: Name two other ways to check for a power of two and compare them to the bit trick.
Besides n & (n - 1), how else can you test whether n is a power of two?
cards.answer: Repeated division by 2 (O(log n)); counting set bits == 1; n & -n == n (lowest set bit equals n). The n & (n-1) test is O(1) and branch-free.
